name: urweb
why: Ur/Web is a statically typed functional language for the web with type-level tricks for SQL and HTML, rarely seen and genuinely unusual.

brief.what_it_is: Ur/Web is a domain-specific functional programming language for building dynamic web applications backed by SQL databases. Ur is a pure, strict, statically typed language in the ML and Haskell tradition with a richer type system and row-type metaprogramming; Ur/Web adds a standard library and parsing and optimization rules for web and SQL work. The compiler, invoked as urweql, takes Ur/Web source and produces a standalone web server executable, and it also generates JavaScript for the client-side code.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to make well-typed web programs 'not go wrong' in a broad sense: no code injection, no invalid HTML, no dead intra-application links, no form and handler mismatches, no invalid SQL, and no improper marshaling between the browser, server, and database. It also aims to let metaprogramming build whole sub-applications, such as an admin interface for any SQL table, whose safety follows from the types.
brief.how_it_works: Ur's type system, with row types and type-level metaprogramming, carries the guarantees: the standard library's signatures are designed so that well-typed programs cannot commit the listed bugs. The compiler emits object code that does not use garbage collection, and it also emits JavaScript for the client side so the application does not need a second language. The README says the demo's standalone server uses less RAM than the bash shell.

brief.install_notes: Source build is ./configure, make, then sudo make install, with GNU Make required. ./autogen.sh must be run first only when building from a Git checkout rather than a release tarball. Packages exist for Debian/Ubuntu (apt-get) and Homebrew. The README mentions no hardware, accounts, or runtime prerequisites beyond the build tools, and it describes no configuration or first-run steps other than compiling and running the demo.
brief.standout: Few languages try to make web-app safety a property of the type signatures, covering injection, HTML validity, dead links, form-handler mismatches, and SQL validity all at once. The README also claims the same language compiles to a GC-free native server and to client-side JavaScript, which is unusual.
brief.status: unknown. The README gives no release version or date, and I did not check the GitHub commit history or release page. Its Travis CI badge points to travis-ci.org, a domain that has since been retired, which hints the CI setup may be old, but that is an inference and not evidence about current activity.
brief.caveats: The homepage fetch returned only a page title and no readable body, so the homepage added nothing beyond the GitHub README. The language is niche and has a steep learning curve with rich types and row-type metaprogramming. Source builds need GNU Make and, from git, autogen.sh. The README does not state the license or supported platforms beyond Linux packaging and Mac via Homebrew. The reference manual is a PDF, which I did not open.

The Ur/Web compiler also produces very efficient object code that does not use garbage collection.

judge.reason: Ur/Web’s type-level guarantees across SQL, HTML, links, and client-server boundaries make it a genuinely unusual language worth exploring.

entry.title: Ur/Web
entry.tldr: A statically typed functional language for web apps where the type system rules out injection, invalid HTML, dead links and bad SQL.
entry.deeper_look:
Ur/Web is a domain-specific language for web applications backed by SQL databases. Ur itself is pure, strict and statically typed, in the ML and Haskell tradition, but with what the README calls "a significantly richer type system". Ur/Web adds a standard library and compiler rules for web and SQL work. The compiler takes Ur/Web source and produces a standalone web server executable, plus JavaScript for the client-side code, so one language covers both sides.

The point is to make well-typed programs "not go wrong" in a broad sense. The README lists what the types are meant to rule out: code injection, invalid HTML, dead intra-application links, mismatches between forms and their handlers, invalid SQL, and improper marshaling between browser, server and database. The standard library's signatures are designed so that these mistakes fail to type-check instead of failing in production.

The larger idea is row types and type-level metaprogramming. Because a table's columns can be described in the type system, code can be written once and applied to any table. The README's example is a demo with an ML-style functor that builds an admin interface for an arbitrary SQL table, with its safety following from the types. The compiler also emits object code that does not use garbage collection, and the README says the demo server uses less RAM than the bash shell.

try_this.what_happens: Compiles the bundled Hello demo into a standalone server executable.
Starts the compiled server in the background.
Fetches the Hello app's main page from the local server and prints it.

entry.whats_unique: Few languages try to make web-app safety a property of type signatures across HTML, SQL, links and forms all at once. The same language also compiles to a GC-free native server and to client-side JavaScript.
entry.caveats: It is niche with a steep learning curve, and the brief could not confirm how actively it is maintained; the README's CI badge points to a retired domain.
